segments.narration: He printed his own money and San Francisco spent it. Joshua Norton. A bankrupt rice trader who declared himself Emperor of the United States.
September 1859. He hand-delivered the proclamation to a newspaper, which printed it that same evening. Weeks later he abolished Congress by decree.
Congress ignored him. His city did not. Restaurants took his hand-made banknotes, fifty cents to ten dollars, as real currency.
Why would a whole city play along? In 1867 a guard arrested him as insane. The outrage was loud enough that the police chief apologised.
He died on a sidewalk in 1880, broke. Ten thousand people came to view the body — and the bay bridge he had decreed was finally built in 1936.

verdicts.claim: On 17 September 1859 Norton hand-delivered his proclamation to the San Francisco Daily Evening Bulletin, which printed it that evening, and on 12 October 1859 he decreed the abolition of the US Congress.
verdicts.note: 94% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 3 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Norton issued promissory notes in denominations from 50 cents to 10 dollars and some San Francisco businesses accepted them.
verdicts.note: Denominations of 50 cents to 10 dollars, accepted by some restaurants; acceptance was not universal — a bank refused to cash 100 dollars of his notes — so narration says 'restaurants took' rather than 'the city accepted'.

verdicts.claim: In 1867 a special officer arrested Norton for involuntary mental treatment, and after public outrage the police chief ordered his release and apologised.
verdicts.note: 81% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Norton collapsed and died on 8 January 1880; about 10,000 people came to view his body, and he had decreed a bridge linking Oakland and San Francisco, built as the Bay Bridge in 1936.
verdicts.note: Collapsed at California and Dupont Streets, died 8 January 1880; the Chronicle reported about 10,000 viewers. He decreed a bridge or tunnel between Oakland and San Francisco, realised by the Bay Bridge in 1936 — narration claims the decree was fulfilled, not that it caused the bridge. The much-repeated two-mile funeral procession is a later legend and is not used.
